extracted.intended_audience: NLP researchers, conference reviewers, Area Chairs (ACs), Senior Area Chairs (SACs), and authors interested in how conference decisions are made
extracted.subtask_description: First-person account and practical guidance about how Senior Area Chairs (SACs) and Area Chairs produce accept/reject rankings for papers at top-tier NLP conferences, including the criteria, workflow, and tradeoffs involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desk rejection checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial rudimentary checks for potential desk rejection: 'does the paper conform to the page limit and follow the appropriate format? is it anonymous? etc' and fit with the track.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are performed before reviewer assignment; include conformity to format, anonymity, page limit, and track fit. Papers failing these checks can be desk-rejected without full review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer evaluations (scores and textual reviews)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers read the paper and provide their reviews, along with soundness/excitement/reproducibility scores and textual comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both the numeric scores (soundness/excitement/reproducibility) and the written text are used as primary inputs for downstream decisions; numeric scores can be averaged or compared but have known noise and bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author response / rebuttal / author-reviewer discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: When present, the author response or general author-reviewer discussion can change reviewers' assessments and provides additional experimental results or clarifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different conferences have different rebuttal formats (no rebuttal, internal-only, public reviewer-author discussion, with/without PDF updates). Rebuttals may lead to reviewers raising scores or clarifying issues; they should be considered in the meta-review.

rubrics_metrics.name: AC meta-review and recommendation score
rubrics_metrics.description: The Area Chair (AC) reads the reviews (and ideally the paper) and provides a meta-review that summarizes reviews/discussion and gives a recommendation; the AC recommendation also comes with a 1-5 score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meta-reviews synthesize reviewer input and add the AC's judgment. ACs may down-weight or ignore particular reviews they deem harsh or low-quality. The AC recommendation score is one of the quantifiable signals used by SACs.

rubrics_metrics.name: SAC ranking categories (Accept / Borderline / Reject and multi-tier labels)
rubrics_metrics.description: For *ACL conferences the ranking can be: Accept-Main, Borderline-Main-Findings, Accept-Findings, Borderline-Findings-Reject, Reject; for discussion the author simplifies this to a 3-level ranking: Accept, Borderline, Reject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SACs assign each paper to one of these categories when producing track-level rankings. The multi-tier labels capture distinctions like Main vs Findings and fine-grained borderline statuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative scores as ranking inputs (soundness, excitement, AC rec)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only a few criteria are quantifiable for definitive ranking: soundness/excitement scores and the AC recommendation (1-5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While numeric scores are convenient for sorting and detecting outliers, they must be used with caution due to reviewer noise, bias, and variance in reviewing quality. SACs should not rely solely on these numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: SAC independent judgment and reweighting of inputs
rubrics_metrics.description: SACs should form their own opinion by looking at meta-reviews, the reviews, the scores, and ideally the papers themselves, and may decide to weigh some reviews less (e.g., particularly harsh or low-quality reviews).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The SAC role includes actively re-evaluating reviewer/AC input, ignoring clearly bad reviews when justified, and bringing domain-level judgment to final recommendations rather than passively accepting upstream scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thematic diversity and community-benefit considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Among criteria for ranking are thematic diversity considerations and the SAC's views on 'what constitutes publication-worthy material' and 'which works will benefit our community if they are published now, in this venue.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SACs may balance pure scores with diversity and community-impact goals (e.g., promoting different subtopics, methods, or novel directions) when deciding which borderline papers to accept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance rate / quota constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Conferences operate under space/time constraints and historical acceptance-rate expectations (e.g., ~25-35% for *ACL conferences), which impose an additional constraint: the conference will only accept approximately X% of submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance quotas force SACs to rank papers not just by individual merit but relative to the entire pool; this can lead to sound papers being rejected due to capacity limits. SACs should be aware of quotas when prioritizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority scoring for borderline papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Borderline papers receive a priority score (1-5) which is used to produce the final ranking among borderline items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority scores help break ties and order the (often large) set of borderline submissions; SACs should assign these after discussion and use them to build the final ranked list.

rubrics_metrics.name: SAC workflow to produce rankings (division of labor, merging, meetings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical workflow: divide papers (randomly) among SACs, produce initial classifications, merge them, then hold several-hours-long meetings to discuss papers as needed and assign labels and priority scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tools (spreadsheets sorted by average soundness, AC recommendation, average excitement, and SAC recommendation/priority) to identify outliers and inconsistent rankings; collaborative meetings ensure consensus and reduce unilateral errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of spreadsheets and outlier detection
rubrics_metrics.description: A helpful tool is a sheet with all papers sorted by average soundness, AC recommendation, average excitement, and by SAC recommendation/priority to identify 'out of order' papers or potential mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag and double-check papers that appear out of order (e.g., low scores but ranked higher, high soundness but rejected) by re-reading reviews, the AC recommendation, and the paper itself before finalizing decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling disagreements and overturning upstream recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: When reviewers/ACs disagree or produce apparently wrong rankings, SACs should double-check reviews, AC recommendation, and the paper. Examples include high soundness scores that were rejected, or low scores that were accepted due to bad reviews being ignored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SACs may move papers up or down from initial ranks after investigation; justification and consensus in SAC meetings are important. Be ready to correct 'mistakes' identified via cross-checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals policy stance
rubrics_metrics.description: The author does not support instituting appeals (except for possible clerical errors) because authors have incomplete information and SACs/PCs have the bird's-eye view; informal/unofficial appeals create extra volunteer workload.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If appeals are allowed, they should be limited and handled carefully; otherwise the current view is to discourage appeals to avoid overburdening volunteer chairs and to acknowledge authors lack full context about ranking.

rubrics_metrics.name: SAC additional responsibilities beyond ranking
rubrics_metrics.description: SACs also have responsibilities like chasing (meta)-reviews, giving feedback to meta-reviewers, flagging/considering potential ethical issues, and handling differences for short vs long papers and Main vs Findings decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These tasks are part of ensuring review quality and fairness; SACs should monitor missing/low-quality reviews, escalate ethical concerns, and apply different considerations for paper length/venue distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volunteer nature and workload implications
rubrics_metrics.description: The conference decision process relies on volunteer work from PCs, SACs, ACs, and reviewers; producing rankings can take many full working days and additional processes (e.g., appeals) would further increase the burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design processes and policy changes with awareness of volunteer time costs; overly onerous post-decision processes risk discouraging senior researchers from serving in these roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative recommendation: accept sound papers / increase venues
rubrics_metrics.description: Author's suggested ideal: in theory, any sound paper that is thematically relevant should be accepted; 'the only reasonable call is to entirely let acceptance rates constraints go' and to accept more papers or create more venues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a normative proposal rather than an existing rule: accept sound work broadly (e.g., via Findings or more venues) and let downstream impact determine value. Implementation requires institutional change and venue capacity adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveats about numeric score reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Numeric scores must be taken with a grain of salt because many reviewers are overworked, some review in haste, and unconscious biases exist (e.g., junior reviewers tend to be harsher).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use numeric signals for triage/outlier detection but complement them with reading reviews and papers; SACs should adjust for systematic differences in scoring behavior across reviewers/ACs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity / double-blind considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintaining double-blind reviewing (anonymity periods, arXiv timing) is considered important for fairness, though the author questions short anonymity windows and recognizes tradeoffs with fast-moving topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SACs and PC policy should weigh the benefits of double-blind review versus the community's needs for fast dissemination; authors can use arXiv for urgent work but typically after at least one round of review.
